Scenario credit-loss model: methodology and results

creditloss · methodology on a simulated credit-union book · jump-off 2026-09-30 · horizon 13 quarters · all data simulated

Every number below comes from simulated data generated by simulate_data.py. They show what the method produces and how its checks behave; they are not estimates for any credit union.

1. Results in brief

Across the five segments, cumulative credit losses over 13 quarters are C$63m (0.36% of average exposure) in the baseline and C$141m (0.81%) in the severe scenario. About 88% of the severe-minus-baseline gap comes from higher default rates and the rest from weaker collateral. Consumer and commercial books carry most of the dollar loss; residential mortgages, with low current LTVs and mortgage insurance, lose little even with a 28% house-price fall, but their loss rate rises 8-fold because LGD moves from workout costs alone to a collateral shortfall.

2. How supervisors project mortgage and loan losses

All five frameworks reviewed share one structure: a scenario fixes the macro path, a satellite model turns it into default rates, a collateral or loss-severity rule turns defaults into losses, and an accounting layer turns losses into provisions. They differ in granularity and in how much conservatism is imposed by rule.

3. The model

3.1 Segments

Uninsured mortgages, insured mortgages, HELOCs, consumer loans and commercial/CRE. Each segment has its own PD satellite, LGD rule and EAD rule (set in the config). Household books use household sign priors; the commercial book uses business priors.

3.2 Default rates: the PD satellite

logit(DRt) = c + ρ·logit(DRt−1) + Σk βk·xk,t−Lk + εt (1 to 3 drivers)
  • Target. New 90+ day / impaired flow as an annualized share of the opening balance, in logits so projections stay in (0, 1) and shocks act multiplicatively, as in ECB satellites.
  • Candidates. Every series × transform (level, 4-quarter change, y/y %) × lag 0-4 quarters. A literature table gives each series its expected sign by book and the evidence behind it; series with no entry can be screened but cannot enter a model.
  • Screen → cluster → search (the same engine as the companion balance-forecasting model). Univariate |t| controlling for the lag; greedy correlation clustering at 0.85, with a literature "primary" driver (unemployment, house prices, mortgage rate gap; CRE prices and spreads for business) representing its cluster when its |t| is within 80% of the leader; exhaustive search over 1-3 drivers with correct signs, |t| ≥ 1.65, VIF < 5, distinct variables and 0 ≤ ρ < 0.98.
  • Ranking. By dynamic RMSE: the equation rebuilds the whole history from macro drivers alone, feeding back its own forecasts, the way it must under a scenario. The simplest model within 5% of the best wins.
  • Challengers. BMA over the admissible set (BIC weights), the AR(1) benchmark and literature specifications re-estimated on the same data: BoC SAP 2026-12, a TDSA-style ARDL and an ECB/EBA core satellite for household books; BoC CDM-style and Fed CRE-style for commercial.
  • Champion. Chosen by the out-of-sample record (section 4), not by in-sample fit.

3.3 Loss given default

LTVb,t = LTVb,0 · (Bt/B0) / (HPIt+4/HPI0) LGDb,t = workout cost + max(0, 1 − (1 − d − c) / LTVb,t) LGDt = Σb wb · LGDb,t, wb ∝ balanceb · exp(3·(LTVb − mean LTV))
  • Uninsured mortgages: collateral valued at the scenario house-price index four quarters after default (EBA perfect foresight, liquidation lag), balance amortized on an annuity schedule, selling cost c = 8% and distressed-sale discount d = 10% netted from proceeds. Defaults are weighted toward high-LTV buckets, as TDSA allocates defaults to the riskiest buckets.
  • Insured mortgages: lender LGD = residual unreimbursed cost (1%) + (1 − insurer coverage) × collateral shortfall.
  • HELOCs: second lien; recovers only what is left after the amortized first mortgage.
  • Commercial: Frye-Jacobs link, LGD rising with the default rate, anchored at a 30% long-run LGD.
  • Consumer: fixed 75%.
  • Cures: a share of 90+ defaults cure without loss; the cure rate falls as defaults rise (elasticity 0.3).

3.4 Exposure, losses and IFRS 9 provisions

EADt = drawnt + CCF · undrawnt Credit losst = PDqt · EADt−1 · (1 − curet) · LGDt (stress-test loss at default) ECLStage 1 = Σq=1..4 Sq−1 · PD1,q · LGD*q · EADq · (1+EIR/4)−q ECLStage 2 = Σq=1..L Sq−1 · PD2,q · LGD*q · EADq · (1+EIR/4)−q (L = remaining contractual term) ECLStage 3 = GCA3 · LGD* · discount to mid-workout PCLt = (ACLt − ACLt−1) + net write-offst, ACL0 = probability-weighted allowance
  • Balance sheet: static by default (EBA; Fed 2025), with run-off or balance-forecast growth paths as options.
  • Stage engine (creditloss/modelling/ifrs9.py): gross loans are tracked in Stages 1–3 every quarter. Stage 1 → 2 on a significant increase in credit risk (PD above three times origination PD, the EBA rule; borrower PD drift lognormal, calibrated to the reported Stage 2 share), with an optional 30-days-past-due floor; Stage 2 → 1 cures after probation; defaults enter Stage 3; Stage 3 is resolved after a workout period, cured to Stage 2 or written off. Repayments leave the book and, on a static balance sheet, new loans enter Stage 1.
  • Measurement: 12-month ECL in Stage 1, lifetime in Stages 2 and 3, discounted at the effective interest rate. Lifetime is the remaining contractual term (the revolving exception uses a behavioural life). Scenario PDs are used over the reasonable and supportable period, then revert to the long-run average.
  • Probability-weighted ECL at jump-off weights the four scenarios (IFRS 9 5.5.17). Every scenario opens from it, so the first quarter's PCL includes the move to that scenario's own ECL. The Fed-style allowance (next four quarters of losses) is reported alongside.
  • Disclosures: allowance and gross-loan roll-forwards by stage (IFRS 7.35H–35I), coverage ratios, and sensitivity of the ACL to scenario weights and to staging; management overlays, if any, are reported separately.

4. Validation

At every fourth quarter from end-2006, the whole selection is re-run on data available at that date and every model then forecasts 1-12 quarters ahead, conditional on the macro path that actually happened, which is how a satellite is used in a stress test. Champions must capture at least 80% of cumulative GFC defaults out of sample; among those, the lowest error wins.

Three findings. First, on these data the theory-based ECB/EBA core satellite (unemployment level, house-price growth, mortgage rate) beats the data-driven search out of sample in all four household segments, even though the search fits better in sample: the search's lag and proxy choices shift from origin to origin, which is the instability the Fed warns about and the hand-picking risk Gross & Población describe. Second, BMA is not automatically conservative here; it captured the GFC less well than the single best models for mortgages and HELOCs. Third, every model over-predicts the 2020-21 episode (median capture 160% for the champions), because payment deferrals held defaults down; real data would need an intervention dummy or an exclusion window for that period.

One caution on the champion: in the uninsured-mortgage equation the unemployment term has a full-sample t-statistic of only 1.2. It wins on forecast record, but a validator would ask for that term to be defended on theory (the BoC finds labour markets the central driver) or replaced.

In the severe scenario, peak annual default rates reach 3.13% for Commercial / CRE (2.6× jump-off), 3.25% for Consumer (1.5× jump-off), 0.77% for HELOCs (1.9× jump-off), 0.73% for Mortgages, insured (1.7× jump-off), 0.49% for Mortgages, uninsured (1.6× jump-off). Peak LGD reaches 12% on uninsured mortgages and 43% on HELOCs, against workout-cost floors of 2% and 5%.

What drives the severe-minus-baseline gap

Counterfactual substitution: each component is swapped between the two scenarios and the two orderings are averaged (Shapley), so the parts add up to the total. The PD leg is then split by driver by holding one macro series at its baseline path at a time and rescaling to the PD total.

For commercial loans the collateral effect shows up inside the PD leg, because the Frye-Jacobs LGD moves with defaults rather than with a collateral index.

Model risk

The same scenario run through every PD model gives the range below. The spread between models is often as large as the spread between downside and severe scenarios, which is why the champion is chosen on out-of-sample evidence and the range is reported, not hidden.

Probability-weighted ECL at jump-off

Weights: baseline 40%, upside 10%, downside 30%, severe 20%. Weighted performing-loan ECL is C$46.7m against C$38.4m from the baseline alone; the uplift is largest where losses are most non-linear in the scenario (collateral-driven books).

Top-down cross-check

The net charge-off equation (lag + one-quarter-ahead unemployment change, house-price and GDP growth, after TDSA eq. 25 and CLASS) is fitted on historical charge-offs and run on the same scenarios. Cumulative rates over 13 quarters, %:

Bottom-up, baseline Top-down, baseline Bottom-up, severe Top-down, severe
segment
Commercial / CRE 0.716 0.747 2.022 2.084
Consumer 4.279 4.413 6.458 5.758
HELOCs 0.036 0.181 0.444 0.353
Mortgages, insured 0.006 0.011 0.012 0.015
Mortgages, uninsured 0.009 0.044 0.067 0.083

Consumer and commercial reconcile within a few tenths of a point. For mortgages and HELOCs the bottom-up baseline is far below the top-down figure: the top-down equation learned from a history that includes years of falling house prices, while today's book has low indexed LTVs, so the structural LGD sits at its workout-cost floor. With real data, this gap is the first thing to explain: either current LTVs are lower than the history implies, or the LGD floor and cure rate need recalibrating to realized recoveries.

6. Limitations and next steps with real data

  • Replace simulated files with Moody's history and S0-S4 scenarios, and the credit union's default, charge-off and recovery history by segment. Check that the default-rate definition (new 90+ / impaired flow) matches what was reported historically.
  • Calibrate LGD parameters (selling cost, distressed discount, cure rate, workout cost) to realized recoveries, and the LTV-risk slope to observed default rates by LTV band.
  • Credit-union histories are short and few downturns are in them; pooling with sector data (FSRA filings, CBA arrears) or a panel across credit unions, as the BoC does across provinces, would stabilise the satellites.
  • Add the 2020-21 deferral intervention before trusting any coefficient estimated through that period.
  • Second-round effects (credit tightening feeding back into the economy) and the solvency-liquidity link are outside scope, as they are in TDSA.
